claims.text: In regulated manufacturing environments, quality inspection generates the objective evidence—measurements, test results, and documentation—that proves conformance, and Quality Control feeds that evidence into corrective action systems, process improvements, and supplier feedback loops.
Production-stage quality inspection covers four phases: Incoming (IQC), In-Process (IPQC), Final (FQC), and Outgoing (OQC).
Strong quality inspection programs combine trained inspectors, standardized checklists, and real-time data to drive continuous improvement.

Quality inspection is a point-in-time verification that a product meets specifications, while Quality Control (QC) is the broader feedback system that uses inspection data to drive correction and improvement.
In practice, quality inspection is the systematic process of measuring, testing, and documenting whether a product meets its design specifications before it moves forward in the supply chain.
Inspected products can be the components used for production, semi-finished goods, or, most often, finished goods before shipment to a customer.
Quality inspections in precision manufacturing cover five core areas, including physical dimensions and geometric tolerances, material conformity, and performance and functionality.

Quality inspection is defined in the ISO 2859 standard, which is derived from MIL-STD 105 E, as an activity such as measuring, examining, testing or gauging one or more characteristics of a product and comparing the results with specified requirements in order to establish whether conformity is achieved for each characteristic.

The quality inspector usually follows a pre-established checklist based on the product specifications, using it to guide the control process and check whether production conforms to the specifications.
Quality inspections typically take place before, during, and after production.

Quality inspection comprises the stages Incoming Quality Control (IQC), In-Process Quality Control (IPQC), and Final/PSI, each addressing a distinct point in the production lifecycle and applying broadly across industries, plus specialized inspection types used in precision manufacturing that operate within those stages for aerospace, defense, and high-tolerance work.
In quality control, the term inspection refers to the activity of checking products, whereas audit applies to analyzing manufacturing processes and/or systems.

The American Society for Quality (ASQ) defines quality inspection as a verification activity in which one or more product characteristics are examined and compared against specified requirements to assess conformity.
Every effective quality inspection follows five steps: define criteria, sample, inspect, document, then correct.
Checking quality only at the end of production is very risky.
Each test in a quality inspection may require specific training and equipment, for example testing a watch's accuracy.

The Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) provides comprehensive health and safety information on the safe use of hazardous products in Canadian workplaces.
The main components of WHMIS are hazard identification and product classification, labelling, safety data sheets, and worker education and training.
Canada has aligned the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) with the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS).

Aligning WHMIS with GHS provides more comprehensive hazard classification criteria that better indicate hazard severity, includes new hazard classes, makes physical hazard criteria consistent with the Transport of Dangerous Goods (TDG) regulations, and standardizes hazard and precautionary statements and the safety data sheet format with more comprehensive requirements.
